slides.title: From World War I to Russian Civil War
slides.cap: Historical connection: Revolution and imperial collapse
slides.body: World War I shattered the Russian Empire. Battlefield losses, shortages, and collapsing confidence in the tsar triggered revolution in 1917. Russia's withdrawal from the world war did not bring peace: it opened a struggle between the Bolsheviks, anti-Bolshevik forces, national movements, and foreign armies for control of the former empire.

stats.lbl: World War I shattered the Russian Empire. Battlefield losses, shortages, and collapsing confidence in the tsar triggered revolution in 1917. Russia's withdrawal from the world war did not bring peace: it opened a struggle between the Bolsheviks, anti-Bolshevik forces, national movements, and foreign armies for control of the former empire.

slides.title: Bread, War, and Collapse
slides.body: By early 1917, Russia was exhausted by war, inflation, food shortages, and millions of casualties. Demonstrations in Petrograd grew into a mass uprising as soldiers refused to fire on crowds. The imperial state lost control in days. It mattered because the collapse came from both the streets and the army: once soldiers joined the demonstrators, the monarchy no longer had the force needed to survive.
slides.cap: Crowds demonstrating in Petrograd during the February Revolution

stats.lbl: It ended tsarist rule and opened the power vacuum that made both revolution and civil war possible.

slides.title: Dual Power
slides.body: A Provisional Government tried to rule Russia while soviets of workers and soldiers claimed authority in the streets, factories, and barracks. The new government kept Russia in World War I, a decision that deepened its crisis and gave radical parties room to grow. This divided authority made every major decision unstable, because ministers, soviets, soldiers, and workers all claimed a voice in Russia's future.
slides.cap: Members of Russia's Provisional Government in 1917

stats.lbl: It showed that no single government controlled Russia, allowing radical parties to challenge the Provisional Government from inside the revolution.

slides.title: All Power to the Soviets
slides.body: Lenin and the Bolsheviks promised peace, land, and bread. In October, Red Guards and sympathetic soldiers took key points in Petrograd and moved against the Winter Palace. The Provisional Government collapsed with surprisingly little fighting in the capital. The seizure was small in military scale but enormous in political consequence, because it transferred the capital's institutions to a disciplined revolutionary party.
slides.cap: Later Soviet depiction of the storming of the Winter Palace

stats.lbl: It put the Bolsheviks in power and turned Russia's revolution from a broad anti-tsarist movement into a one-party socialist project.

slides.title: A Revolution Becomes a State
slides.body: The Bolsheviks formed a new government, withdrew from the war, and began remaking political life. Opponents saw the seizure of power as an illegal coup; supporters saw it as the birth of workers' rule. Russia was moving toward civil war. The new regime immediately used decrees, committees, and armed force to turn revolutionary slogans into state power.
slides.cap: Bolshevik leaders during the revolutionary period

stats.lbl: It transformed the Bolsheviks from insurgents into rulers, forcing opponents to decide whether to accept, resist, or fight them.

slides.title: An Election the Bolsheviks Lose
slides.body: Russia's long-promised Constituent Assembly finally met in January 1918. The Socialist Revolutionaries won the largest vote, while the Bolsheviks held power in the capital and major soviets. After one day, Bolshevik forces dispersed the assembly. The closure of the assembly convinced many opponents that the Bolsheviks would not allow electoral defeat to limit their authority.
slides.cap: The Tauride Palace, meeting place of the Constituent Assembly

stats.lbl: It destroyed the main democratic alternative after 1917 and pushed political opposition toward armed struggle.

slides.title: Opposition Hardens
slides.body: Moderates, monarchists, liberals, nationalists, and rival socialists increasingly concluded that the Bolsheviks would not share power. What began as political conflict became armed resistance across the former empire. Anti-Bolshevik forces did not share one ideology, but they increasingly shared the belief that compromise with Lenin's government was impossible.
slides.cap: Map of major fronts and factions during the Russian Civil War

stats.lbl: It turned scattered disagreement into organized resistance, giving the civil war its fragmented but dangerous anti-Bolshevik front.

slides.title: Leaving World War I
slides.body: The Bolsheviks promised peace and needed time to survive. At Brest-Litovsk, they accepted harsh German terms, surrendering influence over huge territories in the west. The treaty removed Russia from World War I but intensified anger at home. The treaty bought the Bolsheviks time, but it did so by accepting territorial losses that many Russians viewed as humiliating and illegitimate.
slides.cap: Territorial losses imposed by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk

stats.lbl: World War I fighting ends for Russia
It saved the Bolshevik regime from the immediate pressure of World War I while giving its enemies a powerful charge of betrayal.

slides.title: A Political Weapon for Enemies
slides.body: Anti-Bolshevik forces used Brest-Litovsk as proof that Lenin's government had betrayed Russia. The treaty also opened space for German-backed regimes and nationalist movements, turning the western borderlands into a maze of competing claims. The treaty also encouraged nationalist projects in the borderlands, making the civil war a struggle over empire as well as ideology.
slides.cap: Delegates at the Brest-Litovsk negotiations

stats.lbl: It widened the conflict by linking anti-Bolshevik politics with lost territory, nationalism, and foreign influence.

slides.title: A Legion Stranded in Russia
slides.body: Czech and Slovak soldiers who had fought against Austria-Hungary tried to cross Russia and reach the Western Front. Clashes with Bolshevik authorities escalated into a revolt along the Trans-Siberian Railway, giving anti-Bolshevik governments sudden military protection. Because the legion controlled key railway points, its revolt turned distance and transport into strategic weapons.
slides.cap: Czechoslovak Legion troops in Russia

stats.lbl: It internationalized the civil war and gave anti-Bolshevik governments control of the Trans-Siberian route at a critical moment.

slides.title: The Whites Gain a Front
slides.body: The Legion's control of railway towns helped anti-Bolshevik forces organize in the Volga region, the Urals, and Siberia. For the first time, the Bolsheviks faced a coordinated military threat across enormous distances. The revolt helped create a chain of anti-Bolshevik authority across the Volga, Urals, and Siberia, areas the Reds could not ignore.
slides.cap: The Trans-Siberian Railway connected the eastern fronts of the war

stats.lbl: It gave the White movement territory, supplies, and momentum, forcing the Bolsheviks to fight a true multi-front war.

slides.title: Trotsky Creates an Army
slides.body: The Bolsheviks inherited a collapsing military and rebuilt it as the Red Army. Leon Trotsky used conscription, former tsarist officers, political commissars, and strict discipline to create a force capable of fighting on many fronts at once. Trotsky combined revolutionary loyalty with old military expertise, using former imperial officers under political supervision.
slides.cap: Leon Trotsky used an armored train as a mobile command center

stats.lbl: It gave the Bolsheviks a disciplined national army, one of the main reasons they could defeat more divided enemies.

slides.title: Repression Behind the Front
slides.body: Civil war hardened Bolshevik rule. The Cheka targeted suspected counterrevolutionaries, hostages, deserters, and political enemies. The Red Terror was presented as revolutionary self-defense, but it also established a pattern of coercive state power. Terror was used not only against enemies but also to enforce grain requisitioning, discipline, and obedience in areas behind the lines.
slides.cap: Cheka personnel during the Civil War period

stats.lbl: It showed that Bolshevik victory depended on coercive state power as much as battlefield success.

slides.title: Supreme Ruler in Omsk
slides.body: Admiral Alexander Kolchak took power in Omsk and became the most prominent White leader in Siberia. His armies advanced westward in 1919, threatening the Volga and raising hopes among Allied observers that Bolshevik power might collapse. Kolchak tried to turn Siberia into the center of a restored Russian state, but his regime struggled to win broad popular support.
slides.cap: Admiral Alexander Kolchak, leader of the Siberian White forces

stats.lbl: It represented the strongest eastern White challenge to Bolshevik rule and briefly made Siberia the civil war's decisive front.

slides.title: Advance Turns to Retreat
slides.body: Kolchak's regime struggled with corruption, harsh repression, weak legitimacy, and overstretched supply lines. Red counterattacks pushed his armies back across the Urals and Siberia. By early 1920, Kolchak was captured and executed. As Kolchak's armies outran their supply lines, peasant hostility and Red counterattacks turned the offensive into a collapse.
slides.cap: The eastern front during the Russian Civil War

stats.lbl: It proved that White military advances could not survive without political legitimacy, logistics, and support behind the front.

title: Denikin's Drive on Moscow
sub: The White South Reaches Its Peak

slides.title: The Armed Forces of South Russia
slides.body: General Anton Denikin commanded the strongest White armies in southern Russia. Backed by Cossack forces and Allied supplies, his troops advanced north through Ukraine and the Don region, briefly making Moscow seem vulnerable. Denikin's army threatened Moscow from the south, making it one of the most serious military dangers the Bolsheviks faced.
slides.cap: General Anton Denikin, commander of White forces in southern Russia

stats.lbl: It marked the high point of the southern White campaign and forced the Reds to defend the heartland of their regime.

slides.title: Too Many Enemies, Too Little Trust
slides.body: Denikin's forces fought the Reds, Ukrainian nationalists, anarchists, and local insurgents while refusing meaningful land reform or national self-determination. The offensive lost momentum, and Red counterattacks drove the Whites back toward the Black Sea. Denikin alienated peasants, workers, and national minorities by promising a united Russia while offering little social reform.
slides.cap: Map of Denikin's 1919 offensive toward Moscow

stats.lbl: It revealed the White movement's central weakness: battlefield strength without a political program that could unite the population.

slides.title: A Confused Intervention
slides.body: Britain, France, the United States, Japan, and others intervened for overlapping reasons: reopening the Eastern Front, protecting supplies, evacuating the Czechoslovak Legion, and containing Bolshevism. Their goals were never fully aligned. Allied forces entered Russia for different reasons, including reopening the Eastern Front, protecting supplies, and limiting Bolshevik power.
slides.cap: American troops in Vladivostok during the Allied intervention

stats.lbl: It gave the war an international dimension but failed to create a coherent foreign strategy against the Bolsheviks.

slides.title: Propaganda Gift to the Reds
slides.body: Foreign intervention gave the Bolsheviks a powerful message: the revolution was under attack by imperial powers. The Allies provided supplies and limited troops, but they never committed enough to decide the war and gradually withdrew. Bolshevik propaganda used foreign troops as proof that the Reds were defending Russia from imperialist invasion.
slides.cap: Map of Allied intervention during the Russian Civil War

stats.lbl: It helped the Bolsheviks present themselves as national defenders, weakening the Whites by associating them with foreign powers.

slides.title: War Beyond Russia
slides.body: As empires collapsed, Poland and Soviet Russia fought over the borderlands between them. Polish leader Jozef Pilsudski hoped to build a federation in Eastern Europe, while Bolshevik leaders imagined revolution spreading westward. The conflict with Poland showed that the Russian Civil War was tied to the future borders of Eastern Europe after the collapse of empires.
slides.cap: Polish defenses during the Polish-Soviet War

stats.lbl: It shifted the struggle from internal control to regional order, linking Bolshevik survival with the question of revolution abroad.

slides.title: Miracle on the Vistula
slides.body: In August 1920, Red Army forces approached Warsaw. A Polish counterattack broke the Soviet advance and forced retreat. The war ended with the Treaty of Riga, fixing a border that would shape Eastern Europe until World War II. The Polish counteroffensive stopped the Red Army near Warsaw and shattered hopes for an immediate revolutionary breakthrough into Europe.
slides.cap: Polish forces during the Battle of Warsaw in 1920

stats.lbl: It preserved Polish independence and set a western limit to Soviet power for the next two decades.

title: Wrangel and the Evacuation of Crimea

slides.title: Wrangel Reorganizes the Whites
slides.body: After Denikin's defeat, Baron Pyotr Wrangel took command in Crimea. He tried to reform the White movement, improve discipline, and offer limited land reform, but the strategic situation had turned sharply against him. Wrangel tried to repair earlier White failures by improving discipline and offering limited reforms, but he inherited a shrinking position.
slides.cap: Baron Pyotr Wrangel, commander of the last major White army

stats.lbl: White movement tries to regain legitimacy
It was the last serious White attempt to create a viable anti-Bolshevik government in European Russia.

slides.title: Exile by Sea
slides.body: Red forces broke through into Crimea in November 1920. Wrangel organized a mass evacuation of soldiers and civilians across the Black Sea. The White cause survived only in exile, while Bolshevik control over European Russia became secure. The evacuation preserved lives and created a lasting Russian emigre community, but it also marked the end of organized White resistance in the south.
slides.cap: Evacuation from Crimea after the defeat of Wrangel's army

stats.lbl: Organized resistance collapses in the south
It symbolized the military defeat of the White armies and the beginning of long-term exile for many anti-Bolsheviks.

title: Kronstadt and the New Economic Policy

slides.title: The Sailors Revolt
slides.body: Kronstadt sailors, once celebrated as revolutionary heroes, rebelled against Bolshevik rule and demanded soviet democracy, free trade, and civil liberties. The uprising shocked the regime because it came from within the revolution's own symbolic heart. Kronstadt shocked the Bolsheviks because the sailors had once been celebrated as heroes of the revolution.
slides.cap: Kronstadt sailors, a powerful symbol of revolutionary militancy

stats.lbl: It exposed deep anger inside the revolutionary camp itself and convinced Lenin that War Communism had become politically dangerous.

slides.title: The NEP Begins
slides.body: Civil war victory left the economy devastated and the countryside hostile to grain requisitioning. Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy, allowing limited markets while keeping Bolshevik political monopoly. The revolution survived by retreating economically. The New Economic Policy restored limited markets and small private trade, easing pressure on peasants and reviving parts of the economy.
slides.cap: Market activity returned under the New Economic Policy

stats.lbl: It showed the Bolsheviks retreating tactically from extreme wartime policies in order to keep political power.

slides.title: The Soviet State Emerges
slides.body: By 1921 the Bolsheviks had defeated their largest enemies, but at enormous human cost. Famine, repression, migration, and economic collapse scarred the former empire. The civil war forged the institutions and habits of the future Soviet state. By the early 1920s, the Bolsheviks had defeated their main armies, suppressed rivals, and built institutions that would define Soviet rule.
slides.cap: Major fronts of the Russian Civil War

stats.lbl: Dead from war, famine, and disease
It marks the transition from civil war survival to the creation of the USSR and a durable one-party state.

slides.title: War Summary: Russian Civil War
slides.cap: The end and legacy of the Russian Civil War
slides.body: The Bolsheviks secured the core of the former Russian Empire and founded the Soviet Union, but famine, disease, repression, and combat killed millions beyond the battlefield.
